performers: Philadelphia Orchestra, Leopold Stokowski (Stokowski’s own orchestration)
intro: Stokowski turns the organ’s D-minor flourishes into music for a huge orchestra, with six horns, four trumpets and four trombones. This is the opening disc side of his 1927 recording with the Philadelphia Orchestra.

sections.mNote: Fast flourishes alternate with sustained harmony

cues.title: An organ becomes an orchestra
cues.text: The opening flourishes and pauses come from a piece for one organist. Stokowski spreads them across an orchestra with a vast brass section, two harps and celesta. The familiar D-minor opening now belongs to a roomful of players.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s Los Angeles Philharmonic note gives the instrumentation of Stokowski’s transcription. https://www.laphil.com/works/toccata-and-fugue-in-d-minor-bwv-565-bach-arr-stokowski
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Philadelphia, April 1927
cues.text: On 6 April 1927 Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra record the work at the Academy of Music. The conductor supplies the orchestration as well as the performance. This side carries the opening portion of their recording.
cues.evidence: Swiss Foundation Public Domain transfer, recording metadata: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PDP-CH_-_Philadelphia_Orchestra,_Leopold_Stokowski_-_Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565_-_Bach_-_Hmv-d1428-5-0761.flac. The orchestration is identified in the LA Phil programme note.

cues.title: Runs against held notes
cues.text: The toccata alternates quick runs with chords that make the music wait. In the organ score, long pedal notes hold the floor beneath the hands. Stokowski carries that contrast between moving notes and sustained bass into the orchestra.
cues.evidence: BWV 565, toccata: free figuration over held pedal notes, described by the Netherlands Bach Society, https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-565. The LA Phil note identifies the orchestral transcription.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Disney makes the choice
cues.text: In 1938 Stokowski and Walt Disney discuss music for Fantasia. Stokowski favours Bach’s “Little” Fugue in G minor; Disney wants the Toccata and Fugue. Disney gets his way, and this orchestration acquires a second life on screen.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard, Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note, recounts the 1938 choice of repertoire. https://www.laphil.com/works/toccata-and-fugue-in-d-minor-bwv-565-bach-arr-stokowski

composer.epithet: He supplied Leipzig’s churches with music for twenty-seven years and left keyboard players enough work for a lifetime.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, turned up in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. His cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, already makes two people say different things together: one sings the psalmist’s plea, another a hymn in long notes above it.
